name: Opalite
physical: Associated with comfort for the throat and voice
Kept nearby by many for restful evenings
summary: Opalite is a man-made milky glass with a blue to golden glow, adopted in crystal practice for calm, gentle communication and quiet optimism.
intro: Opalite looks like a moonlit opal: a milky, translucent stone that glows blue against a dark background and turns pale gold or peach when light passes through it. It is not a natural opal at all, but a manufactured glass, sometimes called sea opal or opalized glass, produced in a range of colors including lavender, pink and green. The stones are inexpensive, smooth and tactile, and they are sold as tumbled stones, beads, pendants and spheres. Many people love it for its soft, dreamy glow, and it has become one of the most popular accessible stones in the modern crystal market.
history: Opalite as a crystal-shop item is a modern invention. Manufacturers developed opalescent glass in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries as an inexpensive imitation of opal, and the milky, shimmering material later found a second life in the crystal community. The name opalite has also been used for common opal and for opalized rock, which causes confusion, but the stones sold today as opalite are almost always glass. Because it was never a natural mineral, there is no ancient folklore, but practitioners have built a lively set of modern associations around its calm, moonlit appearance.
meaning: In the crystal tradition, opalite is a stone of gentle communication and hopeful calm. Its blue glow is read as a throat chakra color, and people use it when they feel nervous about speaking, whether in a meeting, a family discussion or an interview. The pale, moon-like shimmer is associated with softness and peace, and many keep it near for nights when worry is loud. Healers who work with manufactured stones say its energy is clean and neutral, helpful for people who feel sensitive to stronger crystals. Traditionally it is associated with relaxation, easy breathing and a restful mood, and it is a favorite among beginners for that reason.
howToUse: Keep a tumbled opalite in your pocket or bag to touch when you need to speak calmly. A pendant resting at the throat is a popular way to wear it. Hold a sphere in both hands for a few slow breaths before a difficult conversation. Place a piece on your nightstand or under your pillow for a soothing bedtime ritual, or add it to a grid with clear quartz and selenite for a peaceful room. Small opalite beads work in bracelets worn on the non-dominant wrist.
care: Opalite is glass, so it is stable in water and sunlight, though a gentle approach protects the surface from scratches. Rinse with lukewarm water and mild soap, then dry with a soft cloth. Cleanse with moonlight, sound, smoke or by resting it on selenite. Avoid sudden temperature changes and sharp knocks, which can chip or crack glass. Store it apart from harder stones such as quartz, which can scratch it.
identify: Opalite is glass, so look for a uniform, milky appearance with a blue glow against dark backgrounds and an orange-gold glow when backlit. It has no play of color like true opal, which flashes multiple hues. Tiny bubbles and a very smooth, slightly cold feel are normal. If a seller claims natural opal at a very low price, it is likely glass. Honest sellers label it as opalite or sea opal and acknowledge it is man-made.

faq.a: No. Opalite is a manufactured glass that imitates the soft glow of opal. Real opal is a natural hydrated silica with a play of color, while opalite has a milky blue or gold shimmer and no color flash.
